<reason>B won by distinguishing discretionary conservation from deprivation, and emergency safeguards from the main policy. A raised legitimate concerns about wealthy users’ responsiveness and administering essential allowances, but repeatedly assumed that other users’ savings must come from vulnerable households despite B’s explicit protections. B also directly answered the timing objection: announced marginal prices influence consumption before billing. A’s categorical claims about bans guaranteeing savings and backstops invalidating pricing remained insufficiently defended.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest exchange began by asking whether A would reject pricing even if it secured sufficient savings while protecting essentials. A answered yes but justified that answer by again assuming vulnerable users bore the cuts. B’s closing exposed the missing link: price-sensitive discretionary consumption is not necessarily essential consumption.</best_rebuttal>
